title: AI co-authored commits: 3 open-source projects in 2023, 686 of 874 in 2026
content:
Counted 27 October 2026
AI agents co-authored commits in 3 open-source projects in 2023. In 2026, 686 of 874
Borehole reads each project's commit history for commits that declare an AI agent as co-author, and its contributing guide, pull-request template and agent instructions for a policy on AI-generated contributions. In 2026, the average project declared an AI agent on 8.9% of its commits, against 1.2% in 2025, and 96 projects declare one on a quarter or more. Of the 984 public projects in its library, 249 state a policy and 737 have AI-declared commits. 206 do both. The counts move as the library grows.
Year by year
A project counts in a year when its history has enough commits that year to say. The average share is across those projects, counting the ones that declare none as 0%.
By when the project began
Projects begun since AI agents started signing commits declare them most.
Policy and practice
No AI-declared commits does not mean no AI was used. It means no commit says so: a declaration is a co-author line the contributor chose to keep, and a rebase can remove it.
Where projects write their policy
The agents commits declare
Among projects that declare any, the median share of commits carrying an AI declaration is under 1%.
Every project with a stated policy
Why it matters in diligence
A buyer asks who wrote the code and on what terms. A stated policy says what the project accepts; declared commits show part of what it took. Neither proves the rest, and a large gap between the two is a question for the people who run the project.
How this is counted
- Each project counts once, from its newest public reading.
- A policy counts when the project speaks about contributions in a file that governs them. A sentence addressed to the reader, or a template heading, does not count.
- A commit counts as AI-declared when it names an AI agent as co-author. Undeclared AI use is invisible here.
- A year's counts take only the projects with enough commits that year to say.
- A project whose history Borehole could not measure counts as not declaring.
Read a project, or your own
The library lists every project counted here. Licence changes and key-person risk are the other counts across it.
Survey a repository: free on public repositories. Private code is read on your own machine by a collector whose source you can read first.

report.summary: Borehole’s survey finds AI-agent co-authored commits spread from 3 open-source projects in 2023 to 686 of 874 measured projects in 2026, exposing policy-practice gaps.
report.background: AI coding agents moved from autocomplete to semi-autonomous contributors that can open pull requests and sign commits. Git’s co-author trailer gives projects a lightweight way to disclose agent involvement, but norms are unsettled. Open-source maintainers must reconcile contribution licences, developer certificate of origin sign-offs, security review and provenance with code produced partly by tools. Borehole’s dataset tracks public repositories’ commit histories and contribution policies, so its counts reflect disclosed AI co-authorship rather than all AI use. The 2023–2026 jump follows wider adoption of tools such as GitHub Copilot, Cursor, Claude Code and Codex-style agents, plus growing pressure from companies doing software due diligence.
key_points: Disclosure is spreading fast. Borehole counted AI-agent co-authors in 3 open-source projects in 2023 and in 686 of 874 projects with enough 2026 commits to measure. The average project declared an agent on 8.9% of commits in 2026, up from 1.2% in 2025; 96 projects declared one on at least a quarter of commits.

Policy trails practice. Among 984 public projects, 737 have AI-declared commits but only 249 state an AI contribution policy, and just 206 do both. That leaves many projects accepting agent-assisted code without a public rule on disclosure, review, licensing or accountability.

Newer projects are more likely to declare agents, while the median declaring project still marks under 1% of commits. Adoption is concentrated: a small set of heavy users pulls up the average, so headline percentages can overstate typical project experience.

The data measures declarations, not AI use. A commit counts only when it names an AI agent as co-author; contributors can omit the line or remove it during rebase. Projects with no declarations may still use AI heavily, so gaps are diligence questions rather than proof of clean code.
report.impact: For the AI industry, disclosed co-authorship is becoming a provenance signal, but weak standards make it unreliable. Agent vendors and coding tools may face pressure to generate verifiable attribution and audit logs, while maintainers need clearer contribution rules. Developers should expect questions about which agent, model or prompt produced code, and whether licence and security obligations were met. Regular users ultimately depend on maintainers catching AI-generated bugs, vulnerabilities or licence contamination. Buyers doing technical due diligence will compare stated policies with commit evidence; large mismatches invite deeper review. The likely direction is automated policy checks, signed provenance and repo-level AI-use declarations, though privacy and false-negative risks remain.
report.tools: Follow Borehole’s public library and repository survey to compare policies with commit history. Git’s built-in interpret-trailers and Co-authored-by conventions are the underlying disclosure mechanism. For governance, watch OpenSSF Scorecard and AllStar for repository policy enforcement, CLA Assistant for contribution agreements, and SPDX or SLSA-style provenance formats for recording how code was produced. Teams can trial Borehole’s free public-repo survey and run its readable collector locally for private code before adopting any policy.
